newsitem.title: THAILAND: Burma democractic party still struggling after 8 yrs.
newsitem.headline: Burma democractic party still struggling after 8 yrs.

text.p: Eight years after its birth amid unprecedented protest against military rule, Burma's National League for Democracy, led by the charismatic Aung San Suu Kyi, is still floundering, diplomats said on Wednesday.
The ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) had effectively undermined the party's support by arrests, imprisonment and scare tactics, they said.
The NLD evolved from nationwide demonstrations in 1988 which ended with thousands killed or imprisoned when troops fired on protesters who had flocked to the streets calling for change.
It was set up nine days after the military staged a coup and set up SLORC.
"We were founded in order to work for democracy in Burma," Suu Kyi said recently. "We were founded to prevent dictatorship from coming back."
The NLD started out with a fair amount of freedom, as leaders like Suu Kyi travelled across the country in late 1988 and 1989 to talk about democracy and urge opposition to military rule.
But the party's growth had since been stunted by intimidation, diplomats say.
"It's a desperate situation," said one diplomat when asked about the NLD's progress since 1988.
"There has been a systematic undermining and reduction of effectiveness of the NLD by the SLORC. NLD membership has dropped and SLORC has limited the NLD's ability to manoeuvre."
A key sign that SLORC never really meant to accept opposition was seen after 1990 general elections, organised by SLORC, which the NLD won by a landslide. It was never allowed to assume power.

Suu Kyi, daughter of Burma's revered independence leader, Aung San, had been put under house arrest eight months before the poll was held. After the elections, SLORC arrested many elected NLD members or frightened others into exile.

Many have since been released, but the long years of imprisonment, which often included torture for political prisoners, took its toll and reduced the ranks of vocal democracy supporters, diplomats said.
Suu Kyi, who was released in July 1995 after six years of house arrest, complained recently that SLORC was not allowing the NLD to function as a legally registered organisation.
Party officials were regularly intimidated and the party was unable to hold formal meetings, she said.
Nobel Peace Laureate Suu Kyi has been silenced from making any major attacks against the government by a new law which forbids anyone from disrupting the country's peace and stability.
Diplomats said many NLD supporters were too scared to attend Suu Kyi's weekly speeches at the front gates of her house.
"There's just an atmosphere of repression, fear and intimidation now. SLORC's efforts have worked," one said.
SLORC launched a sweeping crackdown on democracy activists in May, arresting more than 260 elected NLD members ahead of a contorversial party gathering at Suu Kyi's house.
The majority were released after about 10 days, but many were forced to sign declarations agreeing to resign from the party and politics, opposition sources said.
Since May, nearly 70 people have been arrested or charged by SLORC, including nine youths recently detained for distributing pamphlets outside Suu Kyi's house on the weekends.
Last weekend Suu Kyi urged continued support for the NLD.
"When the people voted for the NLD they did so with the meaning of 'we support the NLD'. Voting for us means promising to support our work," she said.
"Our work has not changed. Therefore it is necessary for you to keep on supporting us as you did when you voted for us."
